section.title: The Plague of Hail
section.sectionRationale: The seventh plague forms a full, weighty scene: God's declared purpose in raising up Pharaoh, the warning and the chance to shelter, the devastating hail itself, Pharaoh's fullest confession yet, and his hardened heart once the storm stops.
section.thesis: God explains His purpose plainly, that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth, then sends the worst hail Egypt had ever known, and even Pharaoh's confession, the LORD is righteous, and I and my people are wicked, dissolves the instant the thunder stops.
section.frameNote: Three scenes: God's declared purpose and the warning to shelter livestock; the devastating hail on man, beast, and field; Pharaoh's confession and his hardened heart once the storm ends.

units.label: That My name might be proclaimed

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses, “Get up early in the morning, stand before Pharaoh, and tell him that this is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: ‘Let My people go, so that they may worship Me.
Otherwise, I will send all My plagues against you and your officials and your people, so you may know that there is no one like Me in all the earth.
For by this time I could have stretched out My hand and struck you and your people with a plague to wipe you off the earth.
But I have raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power to you, and that My {{shem|name}} might be proclaimed in all the earth.
Still, you lord it over My people and do not allow them to go.
Behold, at this time tomorrow I will rain down the worst {{barad|hail}} that has ever fallen on Egypt, from the day it was founded until now.

So give orders now to shelter your livestock and everything you have in the field. Every man or beast that remains in the field and is not brought inside will die when the hail comes down upon them.’”
Those among Pharaoh's officials who feared the word of the LORD hurried to bring their servants and livestock to shelter,
but those who disregarded the word of the LORD left their servants and livestock in the field.

units.label: Fire flashing in the hail
units.note: the worst storm in Egypt's history

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward heaven, so that hail may fall on all the land of Egypt, on man and beast and every plant of the field throughout the land of Egypt.”
So Moses stretched out his staff toward heaven, and the LORD sent thunder and hail, and lightning struck the earth. So the LORD rained down hail upon the land of Egypt.
The hail fell and the lightning continued flashing through it. The hail was so severe that nothing like it had ever been seen in all the land of Egypt from the time it became a nation.
Throughout the land of Egypt, the hail struck down everything in the field, both man and beast; it beat down every plant of the field and stripped every tree.
The only place where it did not hail was in the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived.
Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron. “This time I have sinned,” he said. “The LORD is righteous, and I and my people are wicked.
Pray to the LORD, for there has been enough of God's thunder and hail. I will let you go; you do not need to stay any longer.”
Moses said to him, “When I have left the city, I will spread out my hands to the LORD. The thunder will cease, and there will be no more hail, so that you may know that the earth is the LORD's.
But as for you and your officials, I know that you still do not fear the LORD our God.”
Now the flax and barley were destroyed, since the barley was ripe and the flax was in bloom;
but the wheat and spelt were not destroyed, because they are late crops.
Then Moses departed from Pharaoh, went out of the city, and spread out his hands to the LORD. The thunder and hail ceased, and the rain no longer poured down on the land.
When Pharaoh saw that the rain and hail and thunder had ceased, he sinned again and hardened his heart, he and his officials.
So Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not let the Israelites go, just as the LORD had said through Moses.

shem.gloss: Name, standing for a person's whole reputation and revealed character. God's stated purpose in this plague, that His name be proclaimed in all the earth, becomes the very verse Paul quotes in Romans 9:17 to ground his teaching on God's sovereign freedom in mercy and judgment.

barad.gloss: Hail. Paired here with fire flashing within it, an unnatural, terrifying combination the text stresses had never before been seen in Egypt, a direct judgment on Nut, the sky goddess, and Seth, god of storms.

basic.context: This is the seventh plague, and God pauses here to explain His purpose directly to Pharaoh: He could have destroyed Egypt already, but He is raising Pharaoh up to display His power and make His name known worldwide. Then the worst hailstorm in Egypt's history falls, mixed with fire, destroying crops and killing anyone left unsheltered outdoors. Pharaoh confesses his sin more fully than ever before, but the moment the storm stops, he hardens his heart again.
basic.hermeneutics: This is real history, and it contains one of the Bible's most direct statements of God's purpose in judgment, later quoted by Paul in Romans 9 to explain God's sovereign freedom. The passage also shows one of Pharaoh's fullest, most explicit confessions of sin, and still it evaporates the moment relief comes, teaching that words of confession are not the same as a changed heart.
basic.originalLanguages: God says His shem, name, will be proclaimed in all the earth through this contest, the exact verse Paul quotes in Romans 9:17. The barad, hail, mixed with fire, was unlike anything Egypt had ever seen, a direct assault on Egypt's sky and storm deities.
basic.typology: Hail mixed with fire recurs as an image of divine judgment throughout Scripture, appearing again in Revelation 8:7 and 16:21 as end-times plagues, tying this ancient judgment on Egypt to the final judgment on a world that, like Pharaoh, refuses to repent even under devastating pressure.
basic.christ: God's stated purpose, that His name might be proclaimed in all the earth, foreshadows the greater proclamation of God's name and glory accomplished through Christ, whose name is above every name so that at the name of Jesus every knee will bow, Philippians 2:9-10, the ultimate fulfillment of God making Himself known to all the earth.
basic.god: God is sovereign even over raising up a rebellious king for His own purposes, as Paul explains directly from this passage in Romans 9. He is also merciful in the midst of judgment, giving explicit warning so that those who fear His word can shelter their households, distinguishing not only Israel from Egypt but even the fearing from the unfearing within Egypt itself.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 9:17 quotes Exodus 9:16 directly to teach God's sovereign purpose in Pharaoh's hardening. Psalm 78:47-48 and Psalm 105:32-33 both recall this plague of hail and fire. Revelation 16:21 pictures a similar plague of great hail as final judgment.
basic.oneStory: This is the plague where God explains His own purpose most plainly, that His name would be known throughout the earth, and Paul later draws directly on this exact text to teach the whole church about God's sovereign freedom. It anticipates the final judgment of Revelation and the ultimate proclamation of God's name in Christ.

context.literary:
The hail account opens the third and last round of the first nine plagues. Plagues one, four and seven each begin with Moses sent to meet Pharaoh early in the morning, Exodus 7:15, 8:20 and 9:13, while the third, sixth and ninth fall without any warning at all. So the seventh begins a new cycle, and it begins it with the longest speech God addresses to Pharaoh anywhere in the plague narrative, verses 13 to 19, inside the longest of the nine plague accounts.

The speech moves in a careful order: the demand, verse 13; the threat, verse 14; the explanation, verses 15 and 16; the charge, verse 17; the announcement, verse 18; and then, for the first time, instructions for escape, verse 19. A story that had been all confrontation now contains a door. Verses 20 and 21 split Pharaoh's own court in two, those who feared the word of the LORD and those who disregarded it, and the rest of the scene follows both groups into the storm.

Repeated words bind the chapter together. The one Hebrew word for "land" and "earth" runs from "no one like Me in all the earth," verse 14, through "wipe you off the earth," verse 15, to "the earth is the LORD's," verse 29. God's "this time" in verse 14 comes back in Pharaoh's mouth in verse 27, "This time I have sinned." The storm itself is told three times, as command, verse 22, as event, verses 23 to 26, and as a report on the crops, verses 31 and 32. That parenthesis about flax and barley slows the story just before its bitter turn.

The ending mirrors earlier plagues. Pharaoh "saw" that the storm had ceased and sinned again, verse 34, exactly as he saw relief after the frogs, Exodus 8:15. Verse 35 then closes the scene with the refrain that all this happened "just as the LORD had said through Moses," so that even the king's defiance ends up confirming the prophet's word.
context.historical:
Rain is rare across most of Egypt. The land's harvests depended on the yearly rise of the Nile, not on storms, so a violent hailstorm with lightning running along the ground would have been both terrifying and strange. That is why the text twice insists that nothing like it had been seen since Egypt became a nation, verses 18 and 24. Egyptian religion assigned the sky and its powers to gods of its own, and Exodus 12:12 says that the plagues were judgment "against all the gods of Egypt." The hail makes the point without naming a single one of them: the heavens over Egypt answer to the God of the Hebrews.

The note about the crops in verses 31 and 32 opens a small window onto the Egyptian farming year. Flax and barley were early crops, while wheat and spelt ripened some weeks later. The barley was "ripe," the word aviv, which later gives its name to the month of the exodus, "the month of Abib," Exodus 13:4. So the note does two jobs. It fixes the season, placing the storm in late winter or early spring, not long before the Passover, and it explains how the locusts of the next plague could still find something to eat, Exodus 10:5 and 10:15. Flax mattered too, for Egypt was famous for its linen, Ezekiel 27:7, and the storm struck a trade as well as a meal.

Readers sometimes ask where these animals came from after the livestock plague, where "all the livestock of the Egyptians died," Exodus 9:6. That plague was aimed at livestock "in the field," Exodus 9:3, and Hebrew narrative often uses "all" for the whole of the group in view, so animals kept elsewhere, or acquired since, are not ruled out.

The first hearers were the generation that walked out of Egypt. They would have heard this storm as a rehearsal for their own meeting with God, for at Sinai the same "thunder and lightning" came down on the mountain, Exodus 19:16, not to break an empire but to bind a people to Him.
context.canonical:
Israel's worship kept this storm alive. Psalm 78:47-48 remembers how God "killed their vines with hailstones" and "abandoned their cattle to the hail," and Psalm 105:32 adds a sharp irony: "He gave them hail for rain." In a land that rarely saw rain, the rain finally came, and it came as judgment.

From here hail becomes part of the vocabulary of divine warfare. At Beth-horon "the LORD cast down on them large hailstones from the sky," Joshua 10:11, so that the hail killed more than the sword. God asks Job whether he has "observed the storehouses of hail, which I hold in reserve for times of trouble, for the day of war and battle," Job 38:22-23. David's deliverance psalm pictures "hailstones and coals of fire," Psalm 18:12-13, and Isaiah 30:30 and Ezekiel 38:22 use hail and fire for the LORD's judgment on the nations. The same weapon is turned on Israel when it becomes like Egypt: "Hail will sweep away your refuge of lies," Isaiah 28:17, and Haggai 2:17 records a harvest struck with "blight, mildew, and hail, but you did not turn to Me." Pharaoh's failure to turn is not only an Egyptian problem.

Other nations did hear the name, as God said they would. Rahab in Jericho knew what the LORD had done, Joshua 2:9-11, and the Philistines centuries later warned one another not to "harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened theirs," 1 Samuel 6:6.

The New Testament takes the chapter up in two places. Paul quotes Exodus 9:16 in Romans 9:17 to show that God's purposes in history rest on His own free choice, and in Romans 9:22 he speaks of God bearing "with great patience the vessels of His wrath," which is the patience of verse 15. Revelation then draws the seventh plague into the last judgments: "hail and fire mixed with blood," Revelation 8:7, a "great hailstorm" when God's temple is opened, Revelation 11:19, and hailstones of enormous weight under the seventh bowl, when "men cursed God for the plague of hail," Revelation 16:21. The heart that will not bend under the storm is Pharaoh's heart writ large.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to know that the plagues were not simply pressure applied until Pharaoh gave in. They were revelation. Verse 14 states the aim, "so you may know that there is no one like Me in all the earth," and verse 16 widens it to the whole world. Israel was meant to understand that its rescue was the first chapter of a story that would make the LORD's name known among the nations, which is why Exodus 15:14-16 pictures Philistia, Edom, Moab and Canaan trembling when they hear.

He also wanted Israel to see where the real dividing line runs. In this plague the line falls inside Egypt. Some of Pharaoh's own officials "feared the word of the LORD" and acted on it, verse 20, and their servants and animals lived. The difference between life and death was not nationality but response to God's word, which prepares for the "mixed multitude" who left Egypt with Israel, Exodus 12:38.

Finally, Moses wanted Israel to recognise hollow repentance. Pharaoh's words in verse 27 are theologically correct, yet Moses answers, "I know that you still do not fear the LORD," verse 30. Israel would later say the same kind of words, "We have indeed sinned," Numbers 14:40, and then act in the same self will. The chapter teaches that confession which only wants the thunder to stop is not yet fear of God.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The narrative records what God said to one king at one moment in redemptive history. "I have raised you up for this very purpose" is not a key for reading every ruler or every disaster since. Jesus refused to treat a collapsed tower as proof that its victims were worse sinners than others, and turned the event into a call to everyone: "unless you repent, you too will all perish," Luke 13:4-5. Believers should be equally slow to announce which storm is aimed at whom.

Several things do carry forward. God's warnings are meant to be acted on, as the officials who sheltered their servants did, and as Noah did when "warned about things not yet seen," Hebrews 11:7. Repentance is tested by what happens after relief comes, which is why John the Baptist called for "fruit in keeping with repentance," Matthew 3:8. And Moses models something costly: he prays for a king he knows to be insincere, verse 30, because the point of his prayer is that Pharaoh may know "the earth is the LORD's," verse 29.

debates.question: What does Paul mean when he quotes Exodus 9:16 in Romans 9:17-18?

views.label: Sovereign and unconditioned choice
views.case: Paul sets the quotation directly after Jacob and Esau, chosen and passed over before either had done good or bad, Romans 9:11, and he draws the conclusion, "He hardens whom He wants to harden," Romans 9:18. On this reading Pharaoh's role was fixed by God's free decision, and Paul's reply to the objector, "who are you, O man," Romans 9:20, assumes exactly that.

views.label: Judicial hardening of a willing rebel
views.case: Exodus says repeatedly that Pharaoh hardened his own heart, Exodus 8:15 and 8:32, and verse 34 here calls his relapse sin. On this reading God's hardening confirms and hastens a direction Pharaoh freely chose, and Paul's point is that God may use a rebel's rebellion for His purpose without being unjust.

views.label: A question of historical role, not final destiny
views.case: Others note that Romans 9 to 11 concerns Israel's place in God's saving purpose. Pharaoh was "raised up" to a role in history, as the stage on which God's power was displayed, and the passage says nothing directly about his eternal state or anyone else's.

debates.bearing: Exodus holds both sides without embarrassment: the LORD hardens, verse 12, and Pharaoh hardens and sins, verse 34. Paul does not soften the first to protect the second. Whatever the precise relation, the text will not let Pharaoh blame God, and it will not let the reader imagine that Pharaoh ever slipped out of God's hand.

debates.question: Was Pharaoh's confession in verse 27 genuine?

views.label: Political words under pressure
views.case: The confession arrives with a request, "Pray to the LORD, for there has been enough," verse 28, and Moses immediately says that neither Pharaoh nor his officials fear God, verse 30. On this view the words were a negotiating move, spoken to end a storm.

views.label: Real conviction without repentance
views.case: Others think Pharaoh meant what he said while the thunder lasted. He names the LORD as righteous and himself as wicked, which is true. What he lacks is not accurate theology but a turned heart, the "worldly sorrow" that Paul says "brings death," 2 Corinthians 7:10. Saul's "I have sinned," 1 Samuel 15:24, and Judas's "I have sinned," Matthew 27:4, show the same pattern.

debates.bearing: Either way the text judges the confession by what followed: "he sinned again," verse 34. The lesson is not that words of confession are worthless, but that they are meant to lead somewhere, and a sorrow that ends when the danger ends has not yet met God.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 16 turns on the verb he'emadtikha, the causative form of amad, "to stand." Literally God says, "I have caused you to stand." The BSB renders it "I have raised you up," and its footnote offers "have spared you." Both readings fit the context: God could already have wiped Pharaoh out, verse 15, but has kept him standing. The Greek Septuagint took it in the second sense, that Pharaoh had been preserved. When Paul quotes the verse in Romans 9:17 he chooses a different Greek verb, "I raised you up," which stresses God's initiative in giving Pharaoh his place in history. Paul does follow the Septuagint in the next phrase, "that I might display My power in you," where the Hebrew reads "to show you My power," as the BSB footnote notes.

The chapter plays on the root kabed, "to be heavy." The hail is "very heavy," kaved meod, in verses 18 and 24, which the BSB renders "the worst hail" and "so severe." Pharaoh then makes his own heart heavy in verse 34; the BSB footnote at Exodus 9:7 notes that the verb there and in verse 34 means "made heavy." The same root gives kavod, glory, and when God says in Exodus 14:4 and 14:17 that He will "gain honor" over Pharaoh, He uses it again. Pharaoh piles weight on his heart, God piles weight on his land, and in the end the weight of glory rests on the LORD. Many readers also note that Egyptian funerary texts pictured the heart being weighed in the judgment of the dead, which would make a "heavy" heart an ominous image for an Egyptian king. In verse 35, by contrast, the verb is chazaq, "to be strong," which the footnote at verse 12 renders "stiffened or strengthened."

The word translated "thunder" is qolot, simply the plural of qol, "voice." Pharaoh's "enough of God's thunder," verse 28, is literally "enough of the voices of God." Psalm 29 makes the same connection, "the God of glory thunders," Psalm 29:3, and the same word is used at Sinai, Exodus 19:16.

Verse 24 says the lightning "continued flashing" through the hail. The Hebrew phrase, fire mitlaqqachat, uses a reflexive form of the verb "to take," fire taking hold of itself, flashing back and forth. Ezekiel uses the same expression for the storm that carries the glory of God, "fire flashing back and forth," Ezekiel 1:4. The storm over Egypt is described in the language of theophany. Verse 23 adds that fire "went" or "walked" to the earth, as if the lightning itself were on the move.

Pharaoh's confession borrows the vocabulary of the law court. Tsaddiq, "righteous," and resha'im, "wicked," are the words for the party found in the right and the party found guilty, as in Deuteronomy 25:1, where judges acquit "the innocent" and condemn "the guilty." Pharaoh is not merely feeling sorry; he is pronouncing a verdict on himself, which makes verse 34 all the more damning.

Two smaller phrases carry weight. The officials who ignored the warning are literally those who "did not set their heart" to the word of the LORD, verse 21, so the chapter's heart language reaches beyond Pharaoh. And "you lord it over My people," verse 17, uses mistolel, a reflexive form of a verb used for heaping up a raised road, Isaiah 62:10. Pharaoh has built himself up as a barrier across Israel's way.

typology.type: Shelter from the announced storm, Exodus 9:19-21
typology.fulfillment: God announced the storm a day in advance and told everyone how to live through it. Those who took Him at His word brought their households under a roof and survived; those who shrugged lost everything in the field. Scripture keeps that shape. Isaiah 32:2 pictures the coming righteous king as "a refuge from the storm," and Hebrews speaks of believers as those "who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us," Hebrews 6:18. In Christ the refuge is a person, and the wrath escaped is final, 1 Thessalonians 1:10. The type falls short because Egypt's barns saved lives for a day; Christ saves forever.

typology.type: Hail and fire as the weapons of final judgment, Revelation 8:7 and 16:21
typology.fulfillment: The seventh plague becomes a pattern for the last judgments. The trumpets bring "hail and fire mixed with blood," Revelation 8:7, and the seventh bowl ends with huge hailstones while "men cursed God," Revelation 16:21. The escalation is in scope and finality: not one nation but the whole earth, and no Moses to pray it away. Yet the pattern of the human heart is the same, for they "did not repent," Revelation 9:20. The type points forward to a storm that no hardened heart survives, and so it presses the urgency of the refuge God has provided before that day.

typology.type: The name proclaimed in all the earth, Exodus 9:16
typology.fulfillment: God raised up Pharaoh so that His name would be told everywhere, and the story of Egypt was indeed told as far as Jericho and Philistia, Joshua 2:10 and 1 Samuel 4:8. In Christ that purpose reaches its full scope. God has given Jesus "the name above all names," Philippians 2:9, and Paul applies to Him the oath of Isaiah 45:23 that every knee will bow. The disciples are sent to baptize all nations "in the name," Matthew 28:19. The type falls short because Egypt heard the name through judgment alone; the nations now hear it as the only name "by which we must be saved," Acts 4:12.

typology.type: Moses the intercessor who stops the storm, Exodus 9:29 and 9:33
typology.fulfillment: Moses goes out of the city, spreads his hands to the LORD, and thunder and hail cease. He prays even for a king he knows is insincere. Christ surpasses him on both counts. He does not ask for the storm to stop; He rebukes the wind and the sea Himself, and the disciples ask, "Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?" Mark 4:41. And His intercession is not a reprieve that can be abused but a saving work: "He always lives to intercede" for those who draw near through Him, Hebrews 7:25. Moses' prayer bought Egypt a pause; Christ's prayer secures a people.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through its central purpose. God says He acts "that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth," verse 16. Jesus takes up that purpose as His own at the edge of the cross: "Father, glorify Your name!" and the answer comes from heaven, "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again," John 12:28. On the night before He died He could say, "I have made Your name known," John 17:26. After His resurrection the name Egypt was forced to acknowledge is the name Jesus bears. Philippians 2:10-11 takes the LORD's own oath from Isaiah 45:23, "Every knee will bow before Me," and applies it to Jesus, so that the confession Pharaoh was meant to make is finally made "to the glory of God the Father." The difference is that the name now goes out as good news. Isaiah 45:22 had already joined the two: "Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth."

It leads to Christ by contrast of confessions. Pharaoh said the right words, "The LORD is righteous, and I and my people are wicked," but wanted only relief. At the cross another condemned man said almost the same thing, "We are punished justly, for we are receiving what our actions deserve," Luke 23:41, and then turned to the One beside him, "Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom." The difference between the two confessions is not the theology but the turning. The thief did not ask for the pain to stop; he asked for Christ, and heard, "today you will be with Me in Paradise," Luke 23:43.

It leads to Christ as the refuge from the storm. God's warning in verse 19 made a way of escape for anyone who would believe it, and the dividing line fell between those who feared the word and those who did not. The gospel draws the same line around a person: "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life. Whoever rejects the Son will not see life," John 3:36. Those who are justified by His blood are "saved from wrath through Him," Romans 5:9.

It leads to Christ as Lord of the storm. In Exodus the hail begins when Moses stretches out his staff and ends when he spreads out his hands in prayer, but both times it is the LORD who acts. When Jesus stands in a boat and says, "Silence! Be still!" the wind obeys Him directly, Mark 4:39, and the disciples are left asking the question this chapter answers: only the God to whom the earth belongs commands the weather.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The hailstones are not a hidden picture of the cross, and the barns are not coded symbols. The links above rest on the purpose God states in the chapter and on the way the New Testament itself uses it.
study.god:
The chapter opens with God claiming to be incomparable: "there is no one like Me in all the earth," verse 14. Earlier Moses had said the same after the frogs, Exodus 8:10, and Israel will sing it by the sea, "Who among the gods is like You, O LORD?" Exodus 15:11. The claim is not abstract. Egypt had gods for sky, river and field, and each plague has quietly shown that none of them could protect their worshipers. The hail brings that to the heavens themselves. The weather does not belong to a pantheon; it answers to one voice, Psalm 148:8, "lightning and hail, snow and clouds, powerful wind fulfilling His word."

God also reveals His restraint. Verse 15 is a startling sentence: "by this time I could have stretched out My hand and struck you." Every plague so far has been measured. Judgment has been graduated so that Pharaoh has had time to listen, and Paul reads this as patience: God "bore with great patience the vessels of His wrath," Romans 9:22. Divine delay is never weakness. As Peter says, "The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise," 2 Peter 3:9.

He is sovereign over rulers. Pharaoh stands only because God has kept him standing, verse 16. "The king's heart is a waterway in the hand of the LORD," Proverbs 21:1. Yet the text never lets sovereignty erase responsibility. God accuses Pharaoh, "you lord it over My people," verse 17, and the narrator calls his relapse sin, verse 34. God works through human choices without becoming the author of their guilt.

He is merciful in the middle of judgment. No earlier plague came with instructions for escape. This one does, and it is offered to Egyptians. The God who judges Egypt also cares whether an Egyptian servant in the field lives or dies, and He makes His word the shelter. That anticipates Jonah's lesson that God has compassion even on a pagan city "and many cattle as well," Jonah 4:11, and it shows that the fear of the LORD, not birth, is what places a person under His protection.

He answers prayer, even prayer for an enemy. Moses prays, and the storm stops, verse 33. God gives Pharaoh one more experience of grace, knowing it will be abused, so that he "may know that the earth is the LORD's," verse 29. God's kindness is meant to lead to repentance, Romans 2:4, and when it does not, the fault lies with the hard heart, not with the kindness.

For worship, the chapter teaches the right fear of God. It is not the terror that begs the thunder to stop, but the trust that hears God's word and acts on it before the storm arrives, and then keeps trusting when the sky is clear.

crossReferences.note: Paul quotes Exodus 9:16, "I raised you up for this very purpose," and draws the conclusion that God "has mercy on whom He wants to have mercy, and He hardens whom He wants to harden." Paul treats this plague speech as the clearest statement in Scripture of God's freedom in directing history for the sake of His name.

Paul speaks of God bearing "with great patience the vessels of His wrath" in order to make His power known and the riches of His glory known to others. That is the logic of Exodus 9:15-16: God could have ended Pharaoh already, but He kept him standing so that His power and name would be displayed.

"He gave them hail for rain, with lightning throughout their land." The psalm catches the irony of a land that rarely saw rain receiving it as hail, and it adds that the storm "shattered the trees of their country," matching the stripped trees of Exodus 9:25.

Israel's long teaching psalm remembers the hail killing vines and sycamore-figs and the cattle abandoned to the hail and lightning. It shows that the plague was rehearsed in worship as a warning to Israel itself, a people who, like Pharaoh, could forget what God had done.

At Beth-horon the LORD "cast down on them large hailstones from the sky," and more died by hail than by the sword. The weapon God used for Israel against Egypt He uses again for Israel in Canaan, showing that the God of the exodus fights for His people in the land as well.

God asks Job whether he has seen "the storehouses of hail, which I hold in reserve for times of trouble, for the day of war and battle." Exodus 9 is an example of that reserve being opened. Hail belongs to God's armoury, not to chance.

God struck Judah's harvest "with blight, mildew, and hail, but you did not turn to Me." The same failure that marked Pharaoh can mark God's own people. The hail of Exodus 9 is not a story about how bad Egyptians were, but about how hard any heart can become.

At Sinai there was "thunder and lightning," the same words used of the storm on Egypt, and the people trembled. The storm that broke Egypt's resistance returns as the setting for Israel's covenant, teaching Israel that the God who rescued them is the same God whose voice shakes the earth.

The Philistine priests warn their own people, "Why harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened theirs?" Centuries later the story of Egypt's hardened heart is being told in a foreign land, exactly as Exodus 9:16 said God's name would be proclaimed in all the earth.

"Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death." Paul's distinction explains Pharaoh's confession: accurate words of guilt, spoken under pressure, that did not lead to repentance and vanished when the storm ended.

Jesus rebukes the wind and sea and they obey Him. In Exodus the storm stopped when Moses prayed to the LORD; here the storm stops when Jesus speaks. The disciples' question, "Who is this?", finds its answer in the God to whom, as Exodus 9:29 says, the earth belongs.

Under the seventh bowl, huge hailstones fall and "men cursed God for the plague of hail." The last judgment repeats the seventh plague on a world scale, and it exposes the same heart: people who suffer God's judgment and still refuse to turn to Him.

study.oneStory:
In the beginning God separated the waters above from the waters below and set the heavens in order, Genesis 1:6-8. In the hail those same heavens are turned against a king who has set himself against God's people. The plagues run creation backward over Egypt, and in the seventh the sky itself becomes the instrument of judgment. What the fall broke in Genesis 3, the trust between the creature and the Creator, shows up here in its hardest form: a man who hears God's word, sees God's power, says God is righteous, and still will not bend.

Yet the chapter also looks forward to the promise made to Abraham, that "all the families of the earth will be blessed through you," Genesis 12:3. God's stated goal is worldwide: His name proclaimed "in all the earth." The exodus is not a private rescue for one tribe. At Sinai God tells Israel that "the whole earth is Mine," Exodus 19:5, and calls them to be a kingdom of priests in the middle of it. And already, in this chapter, some Egyptians fear the word of the LORD and live.

The prophets take that seed further than anyone in Moses' day could have imagined. Isaiah foresees a day when "the LORD will make Himself known to Egypt," Egypt will worship Him, and God will say, "Blessed be Egypt My people," Isaiah 19:21-25. The nation that heard God's name in hail would one day hear it in blessing. At Pentecost visitors from "Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene" heard the wonders of God declared in their own languages, Acts 2:10-11.

In Christ the name is proclaimed as God always intended. Jesus asks the Father to glorify His name at the cross, and after the resurrection the disciples are sent to all nations to baptize in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, Matthew 28:19. The storm of judgment has not been cancelled, but a refuge now stands open for anyone who will believe God's warning and come in.

The story ends in two ways, and Revelation shows both. For the unrepentant, the hail of Egypt returns on a world scale, Revelation 16:21. For the redeemed, the song changes. Standing beside a sea of glass, they sing "the song of God's servant Moses and of the Lamb," and its climax is the purpose of Exodus 9:16 fulfilled: "Who will not fear You, O Lord, and glorify Your name?" and then, "All nations will come and worship before You," Revelation 15:3-4.

sermon.title: The Hardening of Pharaoh and the Hope of the World
sermon.why: Though preached within Piper's series through Romans, this message works directly and at length through Exodus 9:16, Exodus 7:13, 7:22, 8:15, 8:19, and 9:12, tracing the hardening of Pharaoh's heart across exactly this section of the plague narrative and showing how Paul in Romans 9:17-18 grounds his teaching on God's sovereign freedom in this precise passage.

quiz.q: According to God's own words in verse 16, why did He raise Pharaoh up rather than simply destroying Egypt earlier?

options.text: Because Pharaoh was more righteous than the rest of Egypt.
options.note: The passage gives no indication of Pharaoh's righteousness; his stated purpose is entirely about God's display of power and name.

options.text: Because God had no power over Egypt until this point.
options.note: Verse 15 says God could have already wiped Egypt off the earth, showing He always had full power over the nation.

options.text: To display His power and to make His name proclaimed in all the earth.
options.note: Verse 16 states this purpose directly, a verse later quoted by Paul in Romans 9:17.

options.text: No reason is given for Pharaoh being raised up.
options.note: A specific reason is given plainly and directly in verse 16.

quiz.q: What warning did God give before sending the hail, and who heeded it?

options.text: He gave no warning before the hail fell.
options.note: A specific and detailed warning is given in verses 18 to 19.

options.text: He warned Egyptians to shelter their livestock and servants, and those who feared His word did so.
options.note: Verses 19 to 21 describe this warning and note that some among Pharaoh's own officials heeded it out of fear of the LORD.

options.text: The warning was given only after the hail had already fallen.
options.note: The warning explicitly preceded the hail, giving time to prepare.

options.text: Only the Israelites were warned, with no mention of any Egyptians responding.
options.note: The text specifically notes that some of Pharaoh's own officials responded to the warning by sheltering their people and animals.

quiz.q: How did Pharaoh respond immediately after the hailstorm, in verse 27?

options.text: He confessed, 'This time I have sinned,' and acknowledged that the LORD is righteous.
options.note: This is one of Pharaoh's most explicit confessions in the entire narrative, recorded directly in verse 27.

options.text: He denied any wrongdoing entirely.
options.note: The text records an explicit confession of sin, not a denial.

options.text: He blamed Moses and Aaron for causing the storm unfairly.
options.note: Rather than blaming Moses, Pharaoh explicitly confesses his own and his people's wickedness.

options.text: He made no statement at all.
options.note: His confession is directly and extensively quoted in verse 27.

quiz.q: What happened once the storm stopped, according to verses 34 to 35?

options.text: He asked Moses to make the storm return.
options.note: No such request is recorded; he simply hardened his heart again.

options.text: Pharaoh sinned again and hardened his heart, refusing to let the people go.
options.note: These verses record his immediate reversal despite his earlier confession.

options.text: He had no further reaction after the storm ended.
options.note: His renewed hardening is explicitly and emphatically recorded.

options.text: He kept his promise and released the Israelites.
options.note: The opposite occurred; he broke his word once relief was granted.

quiz.q: How does Paul use Exodus 9:16 in Romans 9?

options.text: He uses it only to discuss Egyptian agriculture.
options.note: Paul's use of this verse is entirely theological, concerning God's sovereignty in mercy and judgment.

options.text: He uses it to argue that Pharaoh was ultimately innocent.
options.note: Paul's argument affirms God's sovereignty in hardening, not Pharaoh's innocence; Pharaoh remains genuinely guilty.

options.text: He quotes it directly to ground his teaching that God has mercy on whomever He wills and hardens whomever He wills.
options.note: Romans 9:17-18 quotes this exact verse as the foundation for Paul's argument about God's sovereign freedom.

options.text: He never references this verse anywhere in his letters.
options.note: Paul quotes this verse directly and prominently in Romans 9:17.

questions: God stated His purpose plainly, that His power and name would be known throughout the earth. How does knowing that God's ultimate purpose in your own trials may be far bigger than your immediate relief change how you pray through hardship?

Some of Pharaoh's own officials feared the word of the LORD and sheltered their households, even while serving a hardened king. Where might you need the courage to respond rightly to God even when those around you, including leaders, do not?

Pharaoh's confession sounded genuine, 'The LORD is righteous, and I and my people are wicked,' yet it evaporated within hours. How can you examine whether your own repentance is rooted in true change of heart rather than a desire for relief from consequences?

Paul draws directly on this passage to teach about God's sovereign freedom in mercy and judgment, a truth many find hard to accept. What is your honest response when Scripture teaches something about God that unsettles you?

God's judgment fell on Egypt's crops precisely when barley and flax were vulnerable, sparing the later wheat and spelt. How does this level of precise timing in judgment help you trust God's precise timing in your own circumstances, even those you might call disasters?

translationNotes.note: The phrase I have raised you up can also be rendered I have spared you, both capturing the idea that Pharaoh's continued existence and rule served God's larger purpose rather than being merely an oversight or delay.

The precise timing of the destroyed and spared crops, barley and flax versus wheat and spelt, reflects accurate knowledge of the Egyptian agricultural calendar, where barley ripens and flax blooms earlier in the growing season than wheat and spelt.
